SHARED WORK (WORK SHARING) UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE PROGRAM — INFORMATION SHEET Prepared for Acme, Inc. ABOUT THIS SHARED WORK (WORK SHARING) INFORMATION SHEET This information sheet describes California's Shared Work (also called "work sharing") Unemployment Insurance Program for Acme, Inc., as it may relate to the work unit described below. Affected work unit: the Fabrication Department Number of employees in the affected unit: 22 Proposed reduction in usual weekly hours of work: 20% Proposed plan effective date: November 1, 2026 The sections below state what California's Unemployment Insurance Code provides about this program. They do not constitute a work sharing plan application, an Employment Development Department approval of any plan, or a determination that the work unit, percentage reduction, or other details entered above meet the statute's requirements. THE STATUTORY DEFINITIONS OF "AFFECTED UNIT" AND "WORK SHARING PLAN" California's Unemployment Insurance Code defines an "affected unit" as a specified plant, department, shift, or other definable unit that includes at least two workers and not less than 10 percent of the employer's regular permanent workforce involved in the unit. A "work sharing plan" is a plan an employer submits to the director of the Employment Development Department for approval, requesting payment of "work sharing compensation" to employees in an affected unit, in lieu of layoffs. The statute separately defines "usual weekly hours of work" as an employee's usual full- or part-time hours when the affected unit is operating on its regular basis, capped at 40 hours and excluding overtime hours. [Verified — checked 2026-09-06] "“Affected unit” means a specified plant, department, shift, or other definable unit that includes two or more workers and not less than 10 percent of the employer’s regular permanent work force involved in the affected unit or units in each week, or in at least one week of a two-consecutive-week period, to which an approved work sharing plan applies." — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC§ionNum=1279.5.) "“Work sharing plan” means a plan submitted by an employer, for approval by the director, under which the employer requests the payment of work sharing compensation to employees in an affected unit of the employer in lieu of layoffs." — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC§ionNum=1279.5.) Known gap: This is California's Shared Work (work sharing) statute, Unemployment Insurance Code section 1279.5, used as evidence of what the statute itself provides for an employer that chooses to submit a plan to the Employment Development Department — not a claim that any specific employer's workforce reduction, or any specific employee's reduced hours, actually is, or is not, covered by an approved work sharing plan. This information sheet does not itself submit, approve, disapprove, modify, or revoke any work sharing plan, and it does not determine that any employer's or employee's own circumstances satisfy this section. No case law is cited in this clause: the topic is governed almost entirely by this statutory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and a CourtListener search attempted this session for California appellate decisions construing section 1279.5 returned a 429 rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) before it could complete, so no case law is cited here rather than relied on from memory. Both quotations below are drawn from the same statutory subsection, section 1279.5(a) — they are presented together as definitions from one source, not as independently corroborating sources. The 10-percent-of-workforce and two-or-more-worker thresholds in the "affected unit" definition mean that a workforce reduction affecting only a single worker, or affecting a smaller slice of the workforce than 10 percent (in every week, or in at least one week of a two-week period), does not fit this statutory definition, regardless of how an employer or employee might otherwise describe the reduction. HOW WORK SHARING REDEFINES "UNEMPLOYED" SO REDUCED-HOUR EMPLOYEES CAN DRAW PARTIAL BENEFITS The statute displaces the ordinary definition of "unemployed" used elsewhere in the Unemployment Insurance Code for employees covered by an approved work sharing plan. For those employees, working fewer than their usual weekly hours because their regular employer is participating in an approved work sharing plan — reducing employment and stabilizing the workforce in lieu of a layoff — itself makes the employee "unemployed" for purposes of this section, regardless of what the general unemployment definitions elsewhere in the code would otherwise require. [Verified — checked 2026-09-06] "Notwithstanding Section 1252 or 1252.2 or any other provision of this part, for the purposes of this section an employee is “unemployed” in any week if the employee works less than their usual weekly hours of work for the employee’s regular employer, as the result of the regular employer’s participation in a work sharing plan that meets the requirements of this section and has been approved by the director, pursuant to which the employer, in lieu of layoff, reduces employment and stabilizes the workforce." — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC§ionNum=1279.5.) Known gap: This is California's Shared Work (work sharing) statute, Unemployment Insurance Code section 1279.5, used as evidence of what the statute itself provides for an employer that chooses to submit a plan to the Employment Development Department — not a claim that any specific employer's workforce reduction, or any specific employee's reduced hours, actually is, or is not, covered by an approved work sharing plan. This information sheet does not itself submit, approve, disapprove, modify, or revoke any work sharing plan, and it does not determine that any employer's or employee's own circumstances satisfy this section. No case law is cited in this clause: the topic is governed almost entirely by this statutory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and a CourtListener search attempted this session for California appellate decisions construing section 1279.5 returned a 429 rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) before it could complete, so no case law is cited here rather than relied on from memory. This clause states the special "unemployed" definition created for this section; it does not restate or verify the text of Sections 1252 or 1252.2, the general provisions this section overrides "notwithstanding." A reader who wants to compare the ordinary unemployment definition against this special one would need to separately consult those sections, which this document does not quote. WHAT AN EMPLOYER'S WORK SHARING PLAN APPLICATION MUST CONTAIN An employer wishing to participate in the work sharing program submits a signed written plan to the director for approval, using an application form the director develops. Among other required content, the application must identify the affected unit and the usual weekly hours of work for its employees, and state the specific percentage by which those hours will be reduced during all weeks the plan covers — a percentage the statute confines to a range of not less than 10 percent and not more than 60 percent. The application must also include an effective date and duration, which cannot extend beyond the end of the 12th full calendar month after the plan's effective date. [Verified — checked 2026-09-06] "A requirement that the employer identify, in the application, the usual weekly hours of work for employees in the affected unit and the specific percentage by which their hours will be reduced during all weeks covered by the plan. The percentage of reduction of usual weekly hours of work for which a work sharing plan may be approved shall not be less than 10 percent or more than 60 percent." — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC§ionNum=1279.5.) The quoted text is one requirement among the nine listed in subdivision (c) of section 1279.5; this clause does not quote the other eight (for example, the required certifications about continuing health and retirement benefits, and about the reduction being in lieu of layoffs), though the body text above summarizes the duration cap from a separate paragraph of the same subdivision. The 10-to-60-percent range is a hard statutory boundary: a plan proposing a reduction outside that range does not fit within what section 1279.5 authorizes the director to approve, and this clause does not address what, if anything, an employer could do about a workforce reduction outside that range. THE DIRECTOR'S 10-WORKING-DAY DECISION DEADLINE AND THE EMPLOYER'S 20-DAY APPEAL WINDOW Once a completed work sharing plan application is received, the director must approve or disapprove it in writing, and communicate that decision to the employer, no later than the close of business on the 10th working day afterward. A disapproval must clearly identify the reasons for it. An employer then has 20 days to submit a request for review of a disapproved plan to a work sharing administrator the director designates for that purpose; that administrator's decision on review is final, though the employer may submit a different plan application afterward. [Verified — checked 2026-09-06] "The director shall approve or disapprove a work sharing plan in writing by the close of business no later than 10 working days from the date the completed plan is received and communicate the decision to the employer. A decision disapproving the plan shall clearly identify the reasons for the disapproval. Within 20 days, the employer may submit a request for review of the disapproved work sharing plan to the director’s work sharing administrator, whom the director shall designate for this purpose." — Cal. PLAN DURATION, EMPLOYER TERMINATION, AND THE DIRECTOR'S REVOCATION POWER An approved work sharing plan expires on the date stated in its notice of approval — either the end of the 12th full calendar month after its effective date, or an earlier date the employer and director mutually agree on. Separately, an employer may terminate its own plan at any time on written notice to the director, and may apply to renew a plan within 10 days after a previously approved plan expires. The director, for the director's own part, may revoke approval of a plan for good cause at any time, by a written order specifying the reasons and effective date of the revocation. [Verified — checked 2026-09-06] "The plan shall expire on the date specified in the notice of approval, which shall be either the date at the end of the 12th full calendar month after its effective date or an earlier date mutually agreed upon by the employer and the director." — Cal. "The director may revoke approval of a work sharing plan for good cause at any time. The revocation order shall be in writing and shall specify the reasons for the revocation and the date the revocation is effective." — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC§ionNum=1279.5.) INDIVIDUAL EMPLOYEE ELIGIBILITY AND THE WEEKLY COMPENSATION FORMULA An individual employee is eligible for work sharing compensation for a given week only if the employee is monetarily eligible for unemployment compensation generally, is not otherwise disqualified, is employed as a member of an affected unit under a plan approved before that week and in effect for it, and remains available for the employee's usual hours of work with the work sharing employer (which can include director-approved skills training). The amount of work sharing compensation payable for a week is set by formula: the regular weekly unemployment compensation amount for a week of total unemployment, multiplied by the percentage reduction in the employee's usual weekly hours of work under the plan. [Verified — checked 2026-09-06] "An employee is eligible to receive work sharing compensation with respect to any week only if the employee is monetarily eligible for unemployment compensation, not otherwise disqualified for unemployment compensation, and both of the following are true:" — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC§ionNum=1279.5.) "The work sharing weekly compensation amount shall be the product of the regular weekly unemployment compensation amount for a week of total unemployment multiplied by the percentage of reduction in the individual’s usual weekly hours of work." — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC§ionNum=1279.5.) THE COMBINED-BENEFITS CAP AND THE 52-WEEK LIMIT ON WORK SHARING COMPENSATION Work sharing compensation is not paid on top of an employee's regular unemployment compensation entitlement without limit. Within a benefit year, an employee's combined work sharing compensation and regular unemployment compensation cannot exceed the maximum entitlement already established for regular unemployment compensation, and an employee cannot be paid work sharing benefits for more than 52 weeks under a work sharing plan. Work sharing compensation paid to an employee is deducted from that employee's maximum regular-unemployment-compensation entitlement for the benefit year. expectedJSON.body: Once a completed work sharing plan application is received, the director must approve or disapprove it in writing, and communicate that decision to the employer, no later than the close of business on the 10th working day afterward. A disapproval must clearly identify the reasons for it. An employer then has 20 days to submit a request for review of a disapproved plan to a work sharing administrator the director designates for that purpose; that administrator's decision on review is final, though the employer may submit a different plan application afterward.

The director, for the director's own part, may revoke approval of a plan for good cause at any time, by a written order specifying the reasons and effective date of the revocation.

expectedJSON.body: An individual employee is eligible for work sharing compensation for a given week only if the employee is monetarily eligible for unemployment compensation generally, is not otherwise disqualified, is employed as a member of an affected unit under a plan approved before that week and in effect for it, and remains available for the employee's usual hours of work with the work sharing employer (which can include director-approved skills training). The amount of work sharing compensation payable for a week is set by formula: the regular weekly unemployment compensation amount for a week of total unemployment, multiplied by the percentage reduction in the employee's usual weekly hours of work under the plan.

expectedJSON.body: Work sharing compensation is not paid on top of an employee's regular unemployment compensation entitlement without limit. Within a benefit year, an employee's combined work sharing compensation and regular unemployment compensation cannot exceed the maximum entitlement already established for regular unemployment compensation, and an employee cannot be paid work sharing benefits for more than 52 weeks under a work sharing plan. Work sharing compensation paid to an employee is deducted from that employee's maximum regular-unemployment-compensation entitlement for the benefit year.
